# Roadmap: icalendar-searcher

**This document is a draft** - it was generated by Claude Opus 5 on 2026-08-27 from
the open issues, the README, the changelog, the code, the sibling projects'
roadmaps and the out-of-tree MoU task list.  It has been only partly reviewed by
the maintainer.  And in any case, **an estimate is an estimate** - the only way to know for
sure how much time a task will take is to actually do it.

**Unlike the sibling projects, the issue tracker is not the source of truth here.**
This repository has exactly one open issue,

the funded scope.  Every item below should be filed as an issue before its work

Every item names a deliverable.  Where an item is *partly* done, it says what
already exists, so the estimate reads as the remaining work rather than as the
whole job.

## Overview

`icalendar-searcher` holds the generic search, filter and sort logic that was split
out of the [`caldav`](https://github.com/python-caldav/caldav) library in November
2025.  A `Searcher` object is both a *representation* of a query - which is what
lets `caldav` translate it into CalDAV XML - and an *executor* of that query
client-side, which is what lets `caldav` fall back to local filtering when a server
cannot answer the query it was given.

That dual role is what makes this a library rather than a function, and it is what
shapes the roadmap: **every feature has to work twice**, once as something a
CalDAV `REPORT` body can express and once as something that runs over
`icalendar.Component` objects in memory, with the two agreeing.  A search that
matches different sets depending on whether the server or the client executed it is
worse than a search that is not supported at all.

The library is deliberately not CalDAV-specific.  `caldav` subclasses `Searcher` as
`CalDAVSearcher`, and
[`calendaring-client`](https://github.com/pycalendar/calendaring-client)'s roadmap
commits to the same reuse - its unified search interface (item 1.1), its local
iCalendar file backend (2.2) and its iCalendar feed backend (2.3) are all specified
to filter through this library "so that filtering behaves as it does server-side".
The goal is that one query object can be pointed at a CalDAV server, a JMAP server, a
local `.ics` file or an issue tracker and give the same answer.

That commitment is worth noting here because it changes *which* parts of this library
matter.  `caldav` uses `check_component()` and `sort()`.  A local-file or feed backend
has no server to delegate to, so it uses `filter()` - which is precisely the part of
this library that has never had a real consumer.  See
[Risks](#a-third-of-the-library-has-never-been-used-in-anger).

### Baseline: what ships today

v1.0.6 was released 2026-05-29.  The `[Unreleased]` section of
[`CHANGELOG.md`](../CHANGELOG.md) holds the `comma_list` consolidation, which ships
as **v1.0.7, which is not charged to the grant**.  It ships first, and everything
below is measured against it.  Unlike the sibling projects, this release is small
enough to be donated: the MoU has no line item for it, and none is claimed.

| | |
|---|---|
| Source, excluding the generated `_version.py` | 1847 lines / 632 statements |
| Tests | 229 passing, 5269 lines |
| Statement coverage | **89%** (`searcher.py` 98%, `collation.py` 89%, `comma_list.py` 84%, `filters.py` **81%**) |
| Filter operators documented in `add_property_filter` | 11 |
| ...of those, implemented | **3** (`contains`, `==`, `undef`) |
| Open issues | 1 |
| Python | 3.10 - 3.14 in CI |
| Downstream consumers | `caldav`, pinned `>=1.0.5,<2` |

What works, and is *not* to be re-estimated as new work: RFC 4791 §9.9 time-range
filtering for all three component types including the full VTODO matrix and
open-ended ranges; recurrence expansion through `recurring_ical_events`, with
exceptions and with `split_expanded`; alarm-range search; the `categories`/`category`
virtual properties with their plural-versus-singular semantics, RFC 7986 multi-line
`CATEGORIES` included; `undef` searches; sorting with defaults for undefined
properties; Unicode and PyICU locale-aware sort collation; and the immutability
guarantees (`check_component()` does not mutate `self`, `filter()` and `sort()` do
not mutate their input).

### Guiding constraints

1. **Correctness before surface area.**  The library's whole value to `caldav` is
   that its client-side verdict can be trusted when the server's cannot.  A wrong
   match is not a cosmetic defect here; it is silently missing or silently extra
   calendar entries in a downstream application.  Phase 1 exists because the review
   that produced this document found one.
2. **The client-side answer and the server-side answer must agree.**  Anything added
   to the operator set has to be expressible in a CalDAV `REPORT`, or has to force
   `caldav` into `post_filter=True`.  This is why Phase 2 is three repositories'
   work, not one.
3. **Don't hoard logic that belongs upstream.**  `icalendar` owns iCalendar parsing
   and property types; `recurring_ical_events` owns recurrence expansion.  Where
   this library is compensating for a gap in either, the fix belongs there, on their
   budget.  Several `TODO`s in `filters.py` are of exactly this shape.
4. **The API is frozen at 1.x.**  The README declares the API stable and `caldav`
   pins `<2`.  Everything in the funded scope is additive or a bugfix; the one
   proposal that is not ([#7](https://github.com/pycalendar/icalendar-searcher/issues/7))
   is deliberately outside it.
5. **Honest documentation of what is untested.**  `filter`, `filter_calendar` and
   `sort_calendar` are AI-generated, covered only by AI-generated tests, and have no
   known production user.  The README says so.  Phase 4 must keep saying so rather
   than quietly upgrading the claim.

## Phase 1: Correctness - order-dependent property filtering (4 hours)

Property filters are documented to be conjunctive: a `Searcher` with two filters
matches components satisfying both.  For the `contains` operator on ordinary
properties this is what happens.  For the `==` operator, and for the comma-list
properties (`category`/`categories`) under any operator, it is not: the matching
loop in `FilterMixin._check_property_filters` returns `True` as soon as *one* filter
matches, and never looks at the rest.

The result is that a search matches or does not match depending on the order the
filters were added:

```python
ev = <VEVENT with SUMMARY "Training session", LOCATION "Oslo">

s = Searcher(event=True)
s.add_property_filter("SUMMARY", "Training session", operator="==")
s.add_property_filter("LOCATION", "Berlin", operator="==")
s.check_component(ev)           # -> matches.  It should not; LOCATION is Oslo.

s = Searcher(event=True)
s.add_property_filter("LOCATION", "Berlin", operator="==")
s.add_property_filter("SUMMARY", "Training session", operator="==")
s.check_component(ev)           # -> does not match.  Same query, opposite answer.
```

The same holds with `categories` as the first filter and any failing filter after
it.  Since the loop walks `_property_operator`, a dict, "the order the filters were
added" is the order the *caller* happened to add them in - so a downstream application
can flip the answer by reordering two lines that look interchangeable.

This is not new: the `==` short-circuit predates the split from `caldav`, and the
comma-list one was carried over verbatim by the `comma_list` refactor, which flagged
it in a comment (`filters.py:237`) as "a latent bug ... left as-is here since this
is a behaviour-preserving refactor".  It is now the top item on this roadmap because
it is a wrong verdict rather than a missing one, and because it reaches every
`caldav` user through the `>=1.0.5,<2` pin.

| Item | Deliverable | h |
|---|---|---|
| 1.1 Conjunctive property filters | All operators AND correctly regardless of insertion order, pinned by tests that add the same filters in both orders; the `filters.py:237` comment removed rather than reworded | 4 |

The fix itself is half an hour.  The rest is the test matrix - every operator against
every property class (ordinary, comma-list plural, comma-list singular, `undef`,
expanded recurrences with `skip_undef`, singular `contains` under a non-`SIMPLE`
collation) in both orders, roughly two hours - plus an
hour to run `caldav`'s own suite against the release candidate and read the fallout,
and half an hour for the changelog and the 1.0.8 release.

## Phase 2: Negated searches and the operator set (4 hours)

`add_property_filter`'s docstring documents eleven operators and accepts three.  The
eight that raise `NotImplementedError` are `!=`, `<>`, `~`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` and
`def`.  The README is honest about this; the docstring is not, and reads as a
feature list.

The funded half of the gap is negation.  It is requested by
[`caldav` #568](https://github.com/python-caldav/caldav/issues/568), which names
this library explicitly as one of its four work items, and it is the only missing
operator with a downstream consumer waiting.  CalDAV can express it - RFC 4791
§9.7.5 has `negate-condition` on `text-match` - so it is one of the few additions
that does not force client-side filtering on every server.

The implementation is small.  `add_property_filter` needs two strings added to a
tuple; `filters.py` needs one `elif` branch beside the `==` one; and
`comma_list.matches()` is already a clean dispatch whose two `NotImplementedError`
sites take a `not` around the positive result.  There is no new matching machinery to
write.

The semantics question is real but it is a *lookup*, not a research project.  Does
`SUMMARY != "x"` match a component with **no** `SUMMARY`?  RFC 4791 answers it:
`negate-condition` is an attribute of `text-match`, which sits inside a `prop-filter`
that already requires the property to be present unless `is-not-defined` is given.  So
`!=` requires the property defined, and "not defined" stays `undef`'s job.  The
comma-list case follows the plural/singular split that already exists for the positive
operators.  Decide it, write it down, test it.

`def` is the trivial inverse of `undef`, already documented, and costs almost nothing
once the above is settled.

**Phase 2 depends on Phase 1.**  A negated filter is only well defined once filters
AND correctly - in today's short-circuiting loop a `!=` filter would be wrong twice
over, and tests written against it would pin the wrong behaviour.

| Item | Deliverable | h |
|---|---|---|
| 2.1 `!=` / `<>` negation | Both spellings implemented for ordinary and comma-list properties, with the undefined-property semantics decided, documented and tested; agreement with the CalDAV `negate-condition` path verified against `caldav`'s XML builder | 3 |
| 2.2 `def`, and truth in the docstring | `def` implemented; the docstring's operator list reduced to what exists, with the rest moved to a documented "not implemented" list matching the README | 1 |

2.1 breaks down as half an hour to settle and write down the semantics, an hour to
implement, and an hour and a half of tests - ordinary and comma-list properties,
plural and singular forms, property present and property absent.

2.2 is kept separate from 2.1 rather than folded into it because it is the one item
here that is pure honesty maintenance: `def` is four lines beside `undef`, and the
rest of the hour goes on making the docstring stop advertising eight operators that
raise `NotImplementedError`.

2.1 lands in three repositories: the operator here, the XML builder and the
`post_filter` fallback in `caldav`, and a probe in `caldav-server-tester` to
establish which servers honour `negate-condition`.  **Only this repository's share
is funded here**; the other two are in those projects' own budgets, and `caldav`'s
roadmap already carries #568.

## Phase 3: Collation (8 hours)

Collation is in better shape than the original task list assumed.  Sorting is done:
`Collation.UNICODE` and `Collation.LOCALE` both work through PyICU, with collator
strength mapped onto `case_sensitive`, and the README documents the Turkish and
Norwegian cases.  Equality comparison under a non-simple collation works too, by
comparing sort keys.

One thing does not work.  Substring matching under `Collation.UNICODE` or
`Collation.LOCALE` silently falls back to Python's `in` operator, so a
locale-collated `contains` search behaves as if no collation had been asked for.

The comment above that fallback (`collation.py:187`) explains it as "PyICU doesn't
expose ICU's StringSearch API".  **That is false.**  PyICU 2.16 exports
`StringSearch`, `SearchIterator`, `USearchAttribute` and `CollationElementIterator`;
wiring one up is about twenty lines.  The comment is AI-written and has been
justifying a silent fallback on a premise nobody checked.

What makes this item hard is what happens once you do wire it up.  ICU collation
strength is a single ladder - PRIMARY compares base letters, SECONDARY adds accents,
TERTIARY adds case - and this library steers it with one boolean, `case_sensitive`,
mapped onto SECONDARY/TERTIARY.  Those are not the same axis, and measured
behaviour shows it:

| needle | haystack | locale | strength | matches |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `muller` | `Müller` | de_DE | PRIMARY | yes |
| `muller` | `Müller` | de_DE | **SECONDARY** (what `case_sensitive=False` selects) | **no** |
| `istanbul` | `İstanbul` | tr_TR | SECONDARY | yes |
| `smorgasbord` | `smörgåsbord` | nb_NO | PRIMARY | **no** |

Three things follow.  First, simply wiring `StringSearch` to the existing strength
mapping would *not* fix the `Müller` case, because case-insensitive is not
accent-insensitive - expressing "ignore case, respect accents" needs
`CASE_LEVEL=ON` at PRIMARY strength, which is a second knob the API does not have.
Second, there is no globally correct answer: `smörgåsbord` does not match
`smorgasbord` under `nb_NO` and that is *right*, because ö and å are distinct
letters in Norwegian rather than decorated o and a.  The answer is locale-dependent
by construction.  Third, `==` under a non-simple collation compares ICU sort keys
and therefore inherits exactly the same conflation - so making `contains` consistent
with `==` may mean changing `==`, which is API-visible behaviour under a frozen 1.x.

The defect is therefore not a missing function.  It is that the API exposes one
boolean where the underlying model has two axes, and that the gap is currently
hidden by a fallback that says nothing.

| Item | Deliverable | h |
|---|---|---|
| 3.1 The collation axes | A decision, written down: which of case-sensitivity and accent-sensitivity the API exposes, how they map onto ICU strength and `CASE_LEVEL`, whether `==` changes with `contains`, how the answer maps onto the CalDAV collation names `i;octet` / `i;ascii-casemap` / `i;unicode-casemap` that `caldav`'s `_collation_to_caldav` already emits, and what is deliberately left locale-dependent; the false comment at `collation.py:187` deleted | 3 |
| 3.2 Collation-aware substring matching | `contains` implemented on ICU `StringSearch` per 3.1, consistent with `==` | 2 |
| 3.3 Collation test matrix | Both operators against de_DE / tr_TR / nb_NO / root, across both axes, including the cases in the table above | 2 |
| 3.4 Collation documentation | The README's collation section rewritten around the axes as decided, saying plainly that the correct answer is locale-dependent | 1 |

3.1 is the item and 3.2 to 3.4 are its consequences, which is why they are listed
separately even though all four are funded.  3.1 is an API decision under a 1.x that
the README declares stable, and it has to be reconciled with what `caldav` already
sends on the wire; getting it wrong is expensive in a way that a late implementation
is not.  If anything in this phase slips, it should be 3.4, not 3.1.

Note that 3.1 may conclude that `==` has to change too.  That is a behaviour change
on a stable API, and if it happens it goes out in 1.1.0 with the operators rather
than quietly in a patch.

## Phase 4: Documentation (32 hours, of which 20 are funded)

The README ends its usage section with "No proper usage documentation has been
written yet, sorry."  That is accurate.  There is no documentation directory before
this file, no built site, no API reference, and no tutorial.  What exists is a
README that is trying to be all four at once, and roughly 900 lines of docstrings
and inline comments that are genuinely good and entirely unpublished.

The README also contradicts itself: it carries **two** `## Maturity` sections, one
saying the library "has not been battle-tested" and the next saying `sort` and
`check_component` have "been through quite some testing".  Both were written by the
same person weeks apart, and a reader has no way to tell which is current.

| Item | Deliverable | h | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4.1 Documentation structure and a published site | A `docs/` tree that builds, published, and built in CI; the README reduced to what a README is for | 8 | **to be requested** |
| 4.2 Usage guide | A task-oriented guide covering query construction, the three component types, time ranges and RFC 4791 §9.9 semantics, recurrence expansion, the `category`/`categories` distinction, collation and sorting | 12 | funded |
| 4.3 Executable examples | A harness that runs every example in the guide as part of CI, so the guide cannot rot the way the README did | 4 | to be requested |
| 4.4 API reference | Generated from the docstrings, with the docstrings corrected where they promise what the code does not do (see 2.2) | 5 | funded |
| 4.5 README repair and peer review | One `## Maturity` section that is true; revisions from at least one reviewer who is not the author | 3 | funded |

4.2 is where most of the value is, and twelve hours is not generous for it.  The
RFC 4791 §9.9 time-range semantics are the single hardest thing about using this
library correctly - the VTODO matrix in particular - and they exist nowhere outside
comments in `filters.py`.  Writing them down as a guide means first reading the
matrix back out of the code and checking it against the RFC, which is most of a day
before a word of prose is written.

4.1 is eight hours because there is nothing to start from: no `docs/` tree before
this file, no tooling chosen, no publishing workflow.

**This is the only phase whose estimate exceeds its budget, and the gap is the point
rather than a rounding error.**  The documentation budget is 20 hours; the work is 32.
The team intends to request the difference - 12 hours - rather than shrink
the estimate to fit, because 20 hours does not produce a site, a guide, an API
reference and a CI harness for a library that currently has none of them.

The MoU allocates the funded 20 hours to **4.2, 4.4 and 4.5** - the usage guide, the
API reference and the README repair.  4.1 and 4.3 are the 12 hours to be requested.

**Name the consequence rather than hide it: as funded, this phase produces
documentation with nowhere to publish it.**  An earlier draft of this roadmap put
the site (4.1) inside the funded 20 and argued that a published guide is useful
without an API reference; the MoU made the opposite call, and the MoU is what was
signed.  The practical effect is that 4.2, 4.4 and 4.5 land in the repository - a
`docs/` directory of Markdown, generated API pages committed alongside it, a
repaired README - and stay there until 4.1 turns them into a site.  That is a worse
outcome than the earlier draft's, not a neutral rearrangement, and it is the reason
4.1 is now **first** in line if the request is granted or if hours free up
elsewhere.

It is also a reason to write 4.2 and 4.4 in a form that survives the move: plain
Markdown or reStructuredText in `docs/`, no tooling-specific markup, so that 4.1 is
a build-and-publish job rather than a rewrite.

4.3 is split out from 4.2 because it is infrastructure rather than documentation, and
because it is the item most likely to expand: examples that run in CI need fixture
calendars, deterministic timestamps and a runner.  Its absence is a real loss - it is
what keeps the guide honest.

It also has a side effect worth naming: examples in a test harness are tests, and
they would exercise `filter_calendar` and `sort_calendar`, which today have no user.
See [Risks](#a-third-of-the-library-has-never-been-used-in-anger).

This phase is carried out by three people (Tobias Brox, and two contributors from
the `icalendar` project), and its funded hours are budgeted separately from the
development ones.  They cannot be moved into Phases 1-3.

## Phase 5: Quality assurance (14 hours)

This is the largest development phase, at nearly half the development budget, and
that allocation is the main judgement call in this roadmap.  The alternative was to
spend it on the operator set and the API ergonomics under
[Beyond the funded scope](#beyond-the-funded-scope) - more surface, more visible to
users.  Guiding constraint 1 says otherwise, and so does the evidence: Phase 1 is a
bug found by reading the code for a day while writing this document, in exactly the
population Phase 5 covers.

The library reports 88% statement coverage across 229 tests, which is a good number
attached to a weak claim.  Coverage says a line ran; it does not say anyone checked
what the line did.  Roughly a third of the public surface - `filter()`,
`filter_calendar()`, `sort_calendar()` - was AI-written, is covered only by
AI-written tests, and has never had a consumer.  Phase 1 exists because a bug of
exactly this kind survived a year, a refactor, and a code comment pointing straight
at it.

| Item | Deliverable | h |
|---|---|---|
| 5.1 Human review of the AI-written surface | `filter`, `filter_calendar` and `sort_calendar` read line by line against the RFC by someone who did not generate them, with the findings filed as issues and the cheap ones fixed | 8 |
| 5.2 `filters.py` coverage | The RFC 4791 §9.9 branches covered, taking the module from 81% towards the rest of the package; the VTODO matrix tested case by case against the RFC text rather than against the implementation | 4 |
| 5.3 Property-type comparison, analysed and filed upstream | A written analysis of what `filters.py:274` asks for - how an `icalendar` property value should compare against a filter value, per property type - filed as an issue against `icalendar` | 2 |

5.1 is deliberately not "write more tests".  Tests written by reading the
implementation pin the implementation, including its bugs; the whole point is to
check the code against RFC 5545 and RFC 4791 instead.  Eight hours is a day of
careful reading for a few hundred statements, and its deliverable is a list of findings -
a phase that ends with "no bugs found" is a successful outcome, not a wasted day.

5.3 is scoped to the analysis and the upstream issue, not to an implementation.  Per
guiding constraint 3, a per-property-type comparison table is the `icalendar`
library's job rather than this one's; what belongs here is a clear statement of what
this library needs from it.  The implementation, wherever it lands, is a prerequisite
for the comparison operators under
[Beyond the funded scope](#beyond-the-funded-scope), which are not funded either.

## Release plan

| Release | Contents | After |
|---|---|---|
| 1.0.7 | *(baseline - `comma_list` consolidation, ships before the funded period, not charged to it)* | - |
| 1.0.8 | Conjunctive property filters | Phase 1 |
| 1.1.0 | `!=`, `<>`, `def`; collation-aware substring matching, and any `==` change the collation decision forces | Phases 2, 3 |
| 1.1.x | The Phase 5 findings, as they are fixed | Phase 5 |
| 1.1.x | Usage guide, API reference and a repaired README, in-repository | Phase 4 (funded part) |
| *unscheduled* | A published documentation site, and executable examples | Phase 4's unfunded 12 hours |

1.0.8 is deliberately its own patch release, ahead of the feature work.  `caldav`
pins `>=1.0.5,<2`, so it reaches users on their next `pip install -U` without any
action on `caldav`'s part, and there is no reason to make a correctness fix wait for
a feature.

1.1.0 is a minor bump because it adds operators.  It should be coordinated with
`caldav`'s #568 work so that the CalDAV XML side and the client-side fallback land
in the same `caldav` release as the operator they depend on.

Phase 5 has no release of its own because its output is findings rather than a
feature.  Whether it produces a 1.1.1 or nothing at all is not knowable in advance,
and a roadmap that promised otherwise would be promising that the bugs exist.

The last row is the honest one: two documentation items have no scheduled release
because they have no funded hours yet.  Dating them before the funding request is
answered would be a work of fiction.

## Effort summary

| Phase | Hours | Funded | Share of dev |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 - Correctness | 4 | yes | 13% |
| 2 - Negated searches and the operator set | 4 | yes | 13% |
| 3 - Collation | 8 | yes | 27% |
| 5 - Quality assurance | 14 | yes | 47% |
| **Development total** | **30** | | |

| | Hours | Funded |
|---|---|---|
| 4 - Documentation *(separately budgeted, three people)* | 32 | 20 h |
| | | **12 h to be requested** |

| | Hours |
|---|---|
| **Total identified in Phases 1-5** | **62** |
| Currently funded | 50 |
| To be requested (documentation) | 12 |

The development side is complete as planned: every item in Phases 1, 2, 3 and 5 is
paid for, and none of them is funded at a fraction of itself in a way that leaves an
unusable stump.  The documentation side is the one carrying a gap.

The shape of the development budget is worth stating plainly, because it is a
choice and not an inevitability: **47% of it goes to quality assurance and 13% to a
correctness fix - 60% on being sure the library is right, against 40% on making it
do more.**  For a library whose entire value to its consumers is that its verdict can
be trusted when a server's cannot, and a third of whose public surface has never had
a human read it against the RFC, that is the correct split.  It is not the split that
produces the most impressive changelog.

### Changes from the original task list

The original list was two development items of 5 hours each, plus the documentation
block - 10 development hours against the 30 now available.

| Original item | Was | Now | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Negated searches | 5 | 4 | Still the only missing operator with a downstream consumer waiting ([`caldav` #568](https://github.com/python-caldav/caldav/issues/568)), but cheaper than the original list assumed.  The matching machinery it needs already exists - two strings in a tuple, one `elif`, and a `not` at two sites in `comma_list.matches()` - and the semantics question RFC 4791 §9.7.5 already answers |
| More work on collations | 5 | 8 | The largest correction, and in the opposite direction from an earlier draft of this document, which cut it to 2 on the strength of a code comment saying PyICU cannot do collation-aware substring search.  PyICU can; the real problem is underneath it.  The API steers a three-level ICU strength ladder with one boolean, `==` and `contains` inherit the conflation differently, and the answer has to reconcile with the CalDAV collation names `caldav` already puts on the wire.  Eight hours is a decision, an implementation, a test matrix across four locales, and a rewritten README section |
| *(new)* Correctness: conjunctive property filters | - | 4 | A confirmed wrong-verdict bug, order-dependent, reaching every `caldav` user through the version pin.  It was not in the original list because it was not known; it outranks both original items on guiding constraint 1 |
| Usage documentation | 20 | 32 | The budget is unchanged at 20 hours; the estimate is not, and this is the one place where the two do not meet.  There is no `docs/` tree, no tooling, no publishing workflow and no API reference, and the §9.9 semantics have to be read back out of `filters.py` and checked against the RFC before the guide can be written.  Split into five deliverables, of which the MoU funds the usage guide, the API reference and the README repair (4.2, 4.4, 4.5); the documentation site and the executable-example harness (4.1, 4.3) are the remaining 12 hours, to be requested |
| *(new)* Quality assurance | - | 14 | The single largest development item, and the one with no precedent in the original list.  A third of the public surface is AI-written, AI-tested and has never had a consumer; Phase 1 is what that population produces.  The 88% coverage figure says those lines ran, not that anyone checked what they did |

Two corrections to the MoU line items themselves, unrelated to the hours:

* The project is called **`icalendar-searcher`**, not `caldav-searcher`.  The name
  was changed before the first release, because the library is deliberately not
  CalDAV-specific - `caldav` is one consumer of it, and `calendaring-client` is
  expected to be another.
* The per-item amounts were `{0}` placeholders, and the header amount was written
  in parentheses rather than braces and covered only the development hours.  Both
  are corrected in the task list; the header now covers the documentation block too,
  the same way `calendaring-client`'s does.

---

## Risks

### The Phase 1 fix changes answers downstream

Making the property filters conjunctive is a bugfix, but it is a *behaviour* change,
and it goes out under a version pin (`>=1.0.5,<2`) that will pick it up
automatically.  Any `caldav` user relying - knowingly or not - on a multi-filter
search returning the union rather than the intersection will see results disappear.

This is the correct direction: the documented, expected and CalDAV-conformant
behaviour is the intersection, and the current behaviour is not merely wrong but
non-deterministic from the caller's point of view.  The risk is not that the change
is wrong, it is that it is silent.

**Mitigation:** the change ships alone, in its own patch release, with a changelog
entry that spells out the before and after rather than saying "fixed filtering".
`caldav`'s test suite is run against the release candidate before it goes out -
`caldav` is the only known consumer, so this is a tractable check rather than a
hopeful one.

### Negated searches are one item in three repositories

Phase 2 is funded here for this library's share only.  The feature is not usable by
anybody until `caldav` builds the `negate-condition` XML and implements the
client-side fallback for servers that do not support it, and it is not *trustworthy*
until `caldav-server-tester` can say which servers those are.  Both of those are
funded, in their own grants - but neither is scheduled against this one.

**Mitigation:** the deliverable here is defined so that it stands alone - an
operator that works client-side, with its semantics documented - rather than as
"negated search works end to end".  If the other two slip, this library still gained
a working operator, and `plann` or `calendaring-client` can use it over local files
without any CalDAV server involved.

The failure mode to avoid is the one `plann`'s roadmap names: two projects each
assuming the other is paying.  The semantics question in 2.1 is the shared part, and
it is budgeted here, on the theory that whoever implements the client-side matcher is
the one who has to answer it anyway.

### A third of the library has never been used in anger

`filter`, `filter_calendar` and `sort_calendar` are AI-generated, tested only by
AI-generated tests, and have no known production consumer - `caldav` uses
`check_component` and `sort`.  Coverage is 88%, which is a real number, but coverage
measures whether a line ran, not whether anyone ever checked that what it did was
right.  `filters.py` is both the least-covered module at 81% and the one holding the
RFC 4791 §9.9 matrix.

**This stops being hypothetical during the funded period.**  `calendaring-client`'s
backends 2.2 and 2.3 have no server to delegate filtering to, so they will drive
`filter()` as their only search path - and they land at roughly hour 100 of that
project's 248-hour plan, i.e. plausibly while this grant is still open.  The first
serious user of the least-exercised third of this library is arriving.

The Phase 1 bug is a sample from exactly this population: it survived a year, a
refactor and a code comment noting it.

**Mitigation:** Phase 5, and specifically 5.1 - a human reading those three methods
against the RFC before `calendaring-client` reads them by running into them.  This is
why nearly half the development budget goes there.  Note what it does *not* buy: 5.1
is eight hours of review with the findings filed, and only the cheap fixes applied.  A
genuinely broken `filter()` would need a fix budget this roadmap does not have, and
would be reported as a known defect rather than quietly absorbed.

`calendaring-client`'s budget has no line for fixing this library either, and its
guiding constraints send bugs found in siblings back to the sibling - so the sequencing
matters: 5.1 should happen before that project's Phase 2, not after.

### Thirty development hours, allocated to the hour

There is no contingency.  A Phase 1 test matrix that uncovers a second
order-dependence, a Phase 3 decision that turns out to require changing `==`, or a
Phase 5 review that finds something substantial in `filter()` all come out of another
item rather than out of a reserve.

Phase 5 is the phase most exposed to this, and uniquely so: it is the only one whose
size cannot be known before it starts, because its deliverable is a list of findings.
Eight hours of review is a defensible estimate; the repair bill it produces is not
estimable at all, and is not budgeted.

Treat the estimates with proportionate suspicion.  Two of them have already been
revised three times, in both directions, each time because a claim in the code or in
the task list turned out not to survive being run against the library.  The Phase 4
and Phase 5 figures have not had that treatment - nothing in them has been measured,
because there is nothing there yet to measure.

**Mitigation:** the phases are ordered by how much it would cost not to do them, so
the plan degrades by dropping its tail rather than by failing in the middle.  Within
phases the same holds: 3.4 is dropped before 3.1, 5.3 before 5.1.

The phases are **not** all independent.  Phase 2 depends on Phase 1, because negation
is not well defined until filters AND correctly.  Phase 5.1 should precede
`calendaring-client`'s backend work rather than follow it.  Phase 3 is independent of
everything.

### Maintainer bandwidth

The primary maintainer has several packages to juggle - five of them funded through
this programme - as well as other priorities and concerns in life.  It is a real risk
that time runs out before the funds do.

**Mitigation:** this is the smallest of the five grants and the one whose items are
most nearly independent of each other, so it is also the easiest to deliver in
fragments.  Phase 1 alone leaves every `caldav` user better off, and it is four
hours.

### Documentation depends on two people who do not maintain the code

Phase 4's hours are shared with two contributors from the `icalendar` project.  That
is a strength for 4.2 - a guide written by someone who had to learn the library is
worth more than one written by its author - and a scheduling dependency for
everything in the phase.

**Mitigation:** the three funded items (4.2, 4.4, 4.5) are independent of each other
and can be picked up by whoever is available, in any order.  What the funding
allocation costs is the ordering advantage: 4.1 is the prerequisite that would have
let the others land on a site as they were written, and it is unfunded, so they land
in the repository instead and are published later in one go.

---

## Beyond the funded scope

Everything below is wanted and none of it is funded.  Rough estimates are given so
the list is costed rather than aspirational - roughly 60 hours in total, on top of
the 12 documentation hours to be requested.  They are order-of-magnitude figures;
unlike the phase estimates, **nothing here has been checked against the code**, and
that caveat travels with them wherever they are quoted.

An earlier draft added "and no funding request is planned for it".  That is no longer
true: this list is the basis of the next funding request, to be made once the current
grant's releases are out.  It is *not* a promise that the request will be made for
all of it, or granted.

Note what this means for the operator set in particular: after this roadmap is
finished, `add_property_filter` will accept six operators (`contains`, `==`, `!=`,
`<>`, `def`, `undef`) out of the eleven its docstring once advertised.  The comparison
operators and the regex one stay unimplemented, and 2.2 makes the docstring say so.

**The rest of the operator set (8 h).**  `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` for date and integer
properties, and `~` for regular expressions.  The comparison operators are the more
useful half - "everything with `PRIORITY` above 5", "everything created since" - and
they are also the half that needs the property-type work that
`filters.py:274` already flags: comparing an `icalendar` property value against a
filter value is not simply `<`, and the type table for it arguably belongs in the
`icalendar` library rather than here - which is why the comparison operators are
costed at 6 hours *on top of* Phase 5.3, not instead of it.  `~` is the other 2, and
cannot be expressed in CalDAV at all, so it would always force client-side
filtering.

**AND/OR subqueries (12 h).**  The class docstring has wanted these since the split: a
`Searcher` currently ANDs everything it holds, and there is no way to express "summary
contains X **or** category is Y".  RFC 4791 has no general-purpose OR either, so this
is client-side-only work with a query-representation design question in front of it -
and that design question is most of the twelve hours.

**A friendlier way to add filters (6 h)**
([#7](https://github.com/pycalendar/icalendar-searcher/issues/7), and
[`caldav` #590](https://github.com/python-caldav/caldav/issues/590)).  Going from
`search(summary="Scrum meeting")` to
`add_property_filter(key="summary", value="Scrum meeting", operator="contains")` was
a real ergonomic regression for `caldav` callers.  A `**kwargs` form is the obvious
fix and the issue already names the trap: keyword names must never be mistakable for
iCalendar property names.  Left out because guiding constraint 4 freezes the API at
1.x, and because `caldav` #590 is the right place to settle what the combined API
should look like.

**Indexing (16 h).**  The README's performance section is explicit that `filter()` walks
the collection one component at a time, and that a server-side user with static data
and many queries would want indexes instead.  Nobody is that user yet.

**Sorting an unbounded expansion (6 h, or 1 h for a guard rail).**  `expand` with an open-ended range yields a
generator, which is fine until something sorts it.  The docstring warns; the code
does not defend.  A streaming or windowed sort would fix it properly; a documented
guard rail would fix it cheaply.

**`FREEBUSY` support (4 h).**  Raised as an open question in the class docstring and never
answered.

**`limit` and `offset` (2 h), and fuzzy matching (6 h).**  Both named as ideas in the
class docstring.  `limit` and `offset` are cheap only if they are honest about
interacting with sorting; fuzzy matching is a research question wearing a feature's
clothes.

**Repository hygiene (1 h).**  Editor leftovers under version control's nose
(`src/icalendar_searcher/#__init__.py.wip#` and several `.bak`/`~` files), and a
stale comment in `pyproject.toml` claiming `caldav`'s CI still exercises this library
with Python 3.9 - `caldav` now requires 3.10 itself.  Not worth a budget line; worth
doing next time somebody is in the file.
